Background: The efficacy of continence surgery with concomitant prolapse repair has been controversial. The “James Lind Alliance”1, a multidisciplinary group of urologists, gynaecologists, academics, patients support groups representatives and scientific societies (such as British Society of Urogynaecologists and British Association of Urological surgeons) has recently highlighted surgical treatment of SUI at the time of concomitant prolapse repair as one of the top 10 research priority areas in urogynaecology. Patients and Methods: A prospective study of 133 women who underwent TO-TVT with concomitant POP repair in the period between April2005 and April2007 (study group). Outcomes were compared to 299 women who underwent TO-TVT as a sole procedure in the same time period within the same institution with the same inclusion and exclusion criteria (control group). The inclusion criteria included women with failed or declined pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT), pre-operative urodynamic SUI or mixed incontinence (MUI) with predominantly bothersome SUI symptoms (selfreported), symptomatic prolapse and SUI. Pre-operative assessment included: urodynamic assessment, completion of validated symptom severity and quality of life (QOL) questionnaires; King's Health Questionnaire (KHQ) & Pelvic Organ Prolapse/Incontinence Sexual Function Questionnaire (PISQ-12). An independent clinician performed the 12-month follow-up. Primary outcome was the patient-reported success rate for SUI on Patient Global Impression of Improvement Questionnaire- PGI-I; defined as “Very Much Improved/Much Improved”. Secondary outcomes included impact on women's QOL and peri-operative complications. Multivariate regression model was used to assess potential risk factors for failure of TO-TVT with concomitant POP repair including the TO-TVT surgical approach used outside-in versus inside-out. Results: 121 women (91%) completed 12 month follow-up; patientreported success rates for TO-TVT with and without concomitant POP repair were 61% and 79.5% at 12 month respectively; p< 0.001 OR 2.995 95%CI 1.690, 5.307 (Table 1). 28 women declined to attend for pad test; 77% (n=72/93) had negative ICS 1-h pad test at 12 month which was significantly lower than 91% (n=210/230) in the control group (p=0.0013, OR 0.112 95%CI 1.57, 5.975). Analysis of KHQ showed median (IQR) postoperative KHQ improvement of 27.5 (-1.7, 43.2) points versus 35.1 (16.4, 53.1) in the study and control groups (Table 1) respectively (p=0.001). Multivariate regression analysis showed BMI>30 kg/m2 (p=0.017, OR0.932 95%CI 0.879, 0.987) and previous continence surgery (p=0.001, OR0.324 95%CI 0.164, 0.638) to be independent risk factors of failure of TO-TVT with concomitant POP repair (Table 2). Results of prolapse surgery in the study group were comparable to the current literature (Table 3). Conclusion: Transobturator tension free vaginal tapes are associated with significantly lower patient-reported success rates in management of symptomatic female stress urinary incontinence when associated with concomitant POP repair. (Table presented).

title: Pulmonary risk assessment for curative therapy
abstract: Introduction Determining the risk for pulmonary resection in patients with lung cancer is challenging, for it entails many aspects, related to both patients' and physicians' perceptions, mentality and expectations. Estimation of cardiac risk Risk assessment for pulmonary resection must include a preliminary cardiac evaluation. Patients deemed at prohibitive cardiac risk should be evaluated and treated as per American Heart Association/American Society of Cardiology guidelines. Those with low cardiac risk or with optimized treatment can proceed with pulmonary assessment. For patients whose exercise capacity is limited, those with a RCRI ≥ 2 or those with known or newly suspected cardiac condition, non-invasive cardiac evaluation is designed to identify the relatively small proportion of patients needing intensified interventions to control heart failure or arrhythmias or to treat underlying myocardial ischemia. Appropriately aggressive cardiac interventions should be instituted prior to surgery in patients who would need them irrespective of the planned surgery. However, prophylactic coronary revascularization prior to surgery in patients who otherwise do not need such a procedure does not appear to reduce perioperative risk. Systematic measurement of DLCO Carbon monoxide lung diffusion capacity (DLCO) has firstly been shown to be a predictor of adverse outcomes after pulmonary resection in the 1980s'. Predicted postoperative DLCO (ppoDLCO), calculated in the same manner as ppoFEV1 has been shown to be a reliable predictor of pulmonary complications and mortality by several investigators. However, until now, DLCO measurement has been mainly reserved to patients with abnormal FEV1 based on the wrong assumption that FEV1 and DLCO are correlated parameters. Indeed, recent papers have shown that the correlation coefficients between FEV1 and DLCO in different subsets of lung resection candidates are invariably below 0.5, indicating poor correlation and that Indeed a more than 40% of patients with normal FEV1 (>80%) may have DLCO < 80%. More studies have demonstrated that a reduced ppoDLCO is a reliable predictor of cardiopulmonary morbidity and mortality not only in patients with reduced FEV1 but also in those with normal respiratory function. Hence there is no justification to reserve this test to selective group of patients with compromised FEV1. This parameter should be measured in all lung resection candidates. The role ppoFEV1 Predicted postoperative FEV1 (ppoFEV1), estimated by taking into account the number of unobstructed segments to be removed during operation, has represented the pivotal parameter in preoperative evaluation. Most recent evidences however have shown its limited role in patients with pulmonary obstructive disease and airflow limitation both in terms of prediction of surgical risk and in the estimation of definitive residual pulmonary function. In this regard, several studies have shown the minimal loss or even the improvement of FEV1 after pulmonary lobectomy in the obstructed patients, questioning the traditional operability criteria mostly based on pulmonary expiratory measures. Nearly one third of COPD patients may actually improve their FEV1 3 months after pulmonary lobectomy for cancer. Owing to the scarce ability to predict the surgical risk in these patients ppoFEV1 should not be used alone for patients selection. Exercise tests: the global physical assessment Exercise testing is increasingly used in the preoperative evaluation of lung resection candidates, since it allows global assessment of the physical fitness. Low-technology tests such as stair climbing test and shuttle walk test can provide only a rough estimation of the aerobic capacity of the patients without providing much information on the causes that are behind the performance. They are typically ideal as screening tests, but for their inherent limited monitoring cannot be used alone to exclude patients from operation. Shuttle walk test: regression analysis showed in one study that 25 shuttles on the shuttle walk test indicate a VO2peak of 10mL/kg/min and for this reason this cut off has been largely used to select patients for operation. However, recent evidences have shown that this test tends to underestimate the exercise capacity at the lower range of VO2max questioning its role in patients' selection for operation. Stair climb: Several studies have shown the ability of stair climbing test to predict surgical risk in candidates for lung resection. A recent large study confirmed in 640 patients submitted to major lung resection that those climbing less than 12 m had a 2-fold and 13-fold higher rates of complications and mortality compared to those climbing higher than 22 m (less than 1% mortality rate). Cardiopulmonary exercise test: Compared to lowtechnology test CPET has several advantages. It is performed in a controlled environment with continuous monitoring of various cardiologic and pulmonary parameters, it is standardized and easily reproducible in different settings, and in addition to VO2peak, which certainly remains the most important parameter associated with exercise capacity, it provides several other direct and derived measures that permit, in case of a limited aerobic reserve, to precisely identify possible deficits in the oxygen transport system. The use of CPET appears therefore of particular importance in those patients deemed at high surgical risk. Indeed the recently published ERS-ESTS functional guidelines recommended its use in patients with cardiac co-morbidity or impaired pulmonary function or both, and in those patients with a reduced exercise tolerance at low-technology exercise tests (such as stair climbing test or shuttle walk test). It is generally accepted that a VO2peak above 20 ml/ kg/min or greater than 75% of predicted represents a safe threshold to undergo any kind of pulmonary resection. On the other hand, a value below 10 ml/ kg/min or lower than 35% of predicted usually contraindicates a major pulmonary resection.

title: Rationale and design of the randomized intervention with CPAP in coronary artery disease and sleep apnea-RICCADSA trial
abstract: Introduction: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is common in coronary artery disease (CAD) and a possible cause of increased mortality. To date, there is a lack of randomized controlled trials to draw the conclusion that all CAD patients should be investigated for OSA and subsequently be treated with continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP). The RICCADSA study is an on-going Swedish single-center (two sites) trial started in December 2005 addressing the impact of CPAP in newly revascularized CAD patients and concomitant OSA (Apnea-Hypopnea- Index [AHI[≥15/h) without daytime sleepiness (Epworth Sleepiness Scale <10). The primary end-point is the combined rate of new revascularization, myocardial infarction, stroke and cardiovascular mortality over a mean period of 3-years. Secondary outcomes include impact of CPAP on cardiovascular biomarkers, cardiac function, maximal exercise capacity and quality of life measures at 3-month- and 1-year follow-up as well as adherence to CPAP treatment in OSA patients. Methods: A total of 244 CAD patients with non-sleepy OSA are randomly assigned to one treatment and one control group. The mean follow- up for patients will be three years. CAD patients with sleepy OSA (n=155) are offered CPAP treatment and included in the trial as positive controls, and non-OSA patients (n=110) as negative controls. The enrollment is expected to be completed in the current month of 2010. Results: Among 1305 revascularized CAD patients, 654 (50.1%) underwent a sleep study by November 30, 2010. OSA was prevalent in 419 (64.1%), of whom 259 (61.8%) were regarded as non-sleepy. Borderline OSA (AHI 5-15/h) was found in 97 (14.8%), non-OSA (AHI<5/h) in 118 (18.8%) and dominantly Cheyne-Stokes respiration in 20 (3.1%), respectively. Conclusion: Our results suggest a markedly increased prevalence of OSA in a revascularized CAD cohort while the majority of those subjects do not report daytime sleepiness. When completed, the RICCADSA- trial will contribute to define the impact of CPAP as a nonpharmacological intervention for CAD patients with OSA regardless of subjective sleepiness.

title: Effects of biofeedback using a home training device on control of stress urinary incontinence: A randomized controlled trial
abstract: Purpose: Stress urinary incontinence (SUI) is a common and distressing condition among parous women that can considerably impact quality of life. Although surgery is widely accepted as the treatment of choice for SUI, conservative management of this condition has received little focus in Japan. The present study compares the effects of pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) with or without biofeedback to control SUI at home. Relevance: If PFMT with or without biofeedback can control SUI, the quality of life for women with SUI would improve. Participants: Twenty-eight women with SUI provided written informed consent to participate in the study. Methods: Participants were randomized to groups that performed PFMT with (BF) or without (PFMT) biofeedback. All patients performed the exercises for 10 minutes twice daily for 12 weeks at home. The BF group received an electromyography-guided biofeedback device and the PFMT group exercised without any device. Assessment parameters included vaginal squeeze pressure, numbers of incontinence episodes and of pads used per day, voiding frequency, the 1-hour pad test, the International Consultation on Incontinence-Short Form (ICIQ-SF) and the King's Health Questionnaire (KHQ). Analysis: As several variables were not normally distributed, pair-wise comparisons were made with the Mann-Whitney U test for between-group comparisons, and the Wilcoxon signed rank test compared changes within groups. All data were statistically analyzed using the SPSS 12.0J program, with p = <0.05 as indicating significance. Results: Maximum vaginal squeeze pressure significantly increased after exercise in both groups (both p < 0.01). The number of incontinence episodes decreased after exercise in both groups, and the difference between before and after exercise reached significance in the BF group (p < 0.05). The number of pads used per day and voiding frequency decreased in both groups, but the differences between before and after exercise in each did not reach significance. Scores for ICIQ-SF and scores for most domains of KHQ significantly decreased in both groups after exercise (both p < 0.05). However, no differences in any assessed parameters between the groups were significant. Conclusions: The present study showed that PFMT with or without biofeedback increases the strength of the pelvic floor muscles, decreased the number of incontinence episodes, and improved the quality of life of women with SUI. However, the additive effects of biofeedback training were not discernable. Implications: These results indicate that PFMT with or without biofeedback is effective for managing SUI.

title: Comparative performance on perceptually regulated 6-minute walk and cycle assessments in patients undergoing coronary artery bypass graft surgery
abstract: Purpose: The purpose of this study was to compare the intensity of, and physiological responses to, perceptuallyregulated six-minute cycle (6MCA) and six-minute walk (6MWA) assessments in patients undergoing coronary artery bypass graft surgery (CABG). Relevance: Timed exercise tests allow ready clinical assessment of functional exercise capacity. As cardiac rehabilitation (CR) programs after CABG often utilize stationary cycling, a measure of cycling capacity, the 6MCA, may provide useful information on CR program efficacy. While the 6MWA has established safety, reliability and responsiveness in patients undergoing CABG, the 6MCA has heretofore not been investigated. Participants: 37 patients awaiting first-time, non-emergency isolated CABG at Westmead Private Hospital between August 2008 and July 2009 (mean age: 66±9 years, 36 men, 1 woman) participated in the study. Exclusion criteria were resting angina, a history of acute myocardial infarction, and musculoskeletal/neurological impairment precluding exercise testing. Methods: Patients performed a 6MWA (pre-6MWA) and a 6MCA (pre-6MCA) on the day before CABG, and again on the day of hospital discharge after CABG (dc-6MWA, dc-6MCA). Assessments were separated by 1 hour, and performed at a patient-perceived 'moderate' to 'somewhat strong' intensity of exertion. Primary outcomes for the assessments were average oxygen consumption (VO2, mL/kg/min), estimated from 6MWA distance (m) and 6MCA work (kJ) using published metabolic equations. Resting and peak heart rates (HRs) for assessments were also recorded from continuous electrocardiographic (ECG) monitoring. Analysis: Paired t-tests were used to compare VO2 and HR data for: (i) pre-6MWA and pre-6MCA; (ii) dc-6MWA and dc-6MCA; (iii) pre-6MWA and dc-6MWA; and (iv) pre-6MCA and dc-6MCA. The Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient was used to assess correlations between: (i) pre-6MWA distance and pre-6MCA work; (ii) dc-6MWA distance and dc-6MCA work; (iii) pre-6MWA distance and dc-6MWA distance; and (iv) pre-6MCA work and dc-6MCA work. Results: Estimated VO2 was significantly higher for the pre-6MCA than the pre-6MWA (14±3 mL/kg/min vs. 11±1 mL/kg/min, p < 0.001). Peak HR was also significantly higher for the pre-6MCA than the pre-6MWA (104±18 beats/min vs. 97±13 beats/min, p = 0.003). Two patients had the pre-6MCA terminated due to cardiac dysrhythmias. Estimated VO2 was significantly higher for the dc-6MCA than the dc-6MWA (13±2 mL/kg/min vs. 10±1 mL/kg/min, p < 0.001), however there was no significant difference in peak HR (108±17 beats/min vs. 107±13 beats/min, p = 0.906). pre-6MCA work was strongly correlated with pre-6MWA distance (r = 0.756, p < 0.001) and dc-6MCA work was moderately correlated with dc-6MWA distance (r = 0.634, p < 0.001). dc-6MCA work was strongly correlated with pre-6MCA work (r = 0.789, p < 0.001), whereas dc-6MWA distance was only moderately correlated with pre-6MWA distance (r = 0.632, p < 0.001). Conclusions: The 6MCA is performed at a higher intensity (estimated VO2, peak HR) than the 6MWA prior to CABG, but can nonetheless be completed safely by the majority of patients completing a 6MWA. Performance on the two assessments is correlated both preoperatively and at hospital discharge, but the 6MCA may more consistently reflect changes in functional exercise capacity. Further investigation of the measurement properties of the 6MCA is warranted. Implications: The 6MCA provides a useful clinical measure of functional exercise capacity for patients undergoing CABG. Assiduous monitoring of ECG and cardiac symptoms is recommended.

title: The predictive value of the timed-up-and-go on disability in older patients 1-year after coronary artery bypass surgery
abstract: Purpose: The purpose of this study was to evaluate the ability of outcome measures used at the time of hospital discharge to predict disability in patients 1-year after coronary artery bypass (CAB) surgery. A secondary purpose was to examine the relationship between disability, exercise self-efficacy, habitual physical activity (PA), and cognitive function in older patients 1-year following CAB surgery. Relevance: Older patients recovering from CAB surgery are especially susceptible to disability and activity restriction. Development or progression of disability often occurs after hospitalization or restricted activity. Hospitalization itself may contribute to progression of disability in vulnerable populations. Participants: This prospective longitudinal study included 27 people, over the age of 65 years, who had undergone CAB surgery and were within 48 hours of hospital discharge. Subjects were consecutive volunteers recruited from a regional medical center. Exclusion criteria included significant cognitive deficit, stroke following CAB surgery, and inability to stand from chair orwalk without >moderate (50%) assistance with or without assistive device. Methods: Multiple domains of functional status were examined just prior to hospital discharge including balance ability (Timed-Up-and-Go (TUG)), endurance/aerobic capacity (2 Minute Walk Test), strength performance (Hand Grip Force, Timed Sit-to-Stand), cognitive function (Telephone Interview of Cognitive Status-Modified), and psychosocial function (Center for Epidemiological Studies Depression Scale). One year follow-up outcomes were obtain via phone interview and included measures of disability (Disability Index), habitual PA (Baecke PA Questionnaire), and exercise self-efficacy (Self Efficacy for Exercise Behavior Scale). Analysis: Data analysis consisted of descriptive statistics, correlations, and regression analysis (P < 0.5). Results: We found correlations between disability and both habitual PA (r =-0.63) and cognitive function (r =-0.38) scores at 1-year following CAB surgery. When evaluating the baseline scores relative to 1-year outcomes, we found correlations between scores on baseline TUG and disability (r = 0.68) and between TUG and habitual physical activity (r =-0.61). Also, cognitive function at hospital discharge was correlated with 1-year habitual physical activity (r = 0.59). Regression analysis of baseline TUG with 1 year disability showed a significant adjusted R square = 0.44 with 95% confidence intervals of -4.75 lower and -0.66 upper. Conclusions: Results suggest that there is a relatively strong relationship between disability and habitual PA level 1- year following CAB surgery. Also, baseline TUG scores are related to both disability and habitual physical activity level 1 year after CAB surgery. Furthermore baseline TUG scores seem to be moderately predictive of 1-year disability in this patient population. Interestingly baseline cognitive function was related to 1-year habitual physical activity possibly indicating that ability to retain health information is related to behavior change, especially in an acute setting. Implications: The TUG may be useful in predicting future disability in older patients after CAB surgery. Being able to identify patients recovering from CAB surgery who are vulnerable to subsequent disability, would allow physical therapists to better identify and advocate for appropriate rehabilitation services following hospital discharge.

title: Microcurrent therapy in the management of chronic tennis elbow: An exploratory investigation
abstract: Purpose: Microcurrent therapy (MCT) involves the application of sub-sensory electric current to body tissue, and can promote tissue repair in bone and skin lesions. Its potential for the treatment of tendinopathies such as tennis elbow has received little attention, and there is uncertainty over which types of microcurrent are most effective. We compared the effects of several forms of MCT on chronic tennis elbow, to establish whether it might promote tendon healing and symptom alleviation, and if one form of MCTis more effective than others. Relevance: A therapy that promotes tissue healing and symptom resolution could be particularly beneficial in the management of tendinopathies, which can be slow to heal and prone to recurrence. Participants: 62 people diagnosed with tennis elbow were assigned to one of four groups, each receiving a different form of MCT. Participants were symptomatic for at least 3 months with no significant improvement in the preceding month. Methods: MCT involved daily home-based treatment for three weeks. Depending on the group, total treatment times were 15-130 hours and current intensities were in the range 25-500'A. All participants were educated about the disorder and given advice about activity modification, and no other treatment was allowed apart from use of medical analgesia and a tennis elbow brace. Outcome measures were sonographic rating of common extensor tendon structural abnormalities and blood flow, pain-free grip strength (PFGS), the Patient-rated Tennis Elbow Evaluation (PRTEE) and a patient-rated Global Change Score. Assessments were conducted at baseline and 3, 6 and 15 weeks later. Analysis: Tests were conducted for baseline equivalence of groups on outcome variables and potentially prognostic indicators. Arepeated measures Analysis of Covariance was used to test for differences between groups over time. T-tests were made for differences within and between groups on changes in all variables over time. Results: All but one participant completed treatment, and all but two were followed through to final assessment. By that time, group mean PFGS had improved by 22-31% of baseline and PRTEE scores by 17-27% of baseline. One group consistently outperformed the others, with 93% much better or completely recovered at final assessment, compared to 47-73% in the other groups. Trends to structural normalisation were seen in all groups but observed changes were small; hyperaemia showed small but consistent patterns of change, suggestive of modulation by MCT. Higher baseline hyperaemia levels were associated with better clinical outcomes. Side effects were minimal and compliance with the treatment protocol was excellent. Conclusions: MCT with monophasic current of intensity less than 50 μA can help alleviate symptoms of chronic tennis elbow; it may promote tendon healing by modulation of tendon blood flow, and its effectiveness depends on initial hyperaemia levels. However, the clinical significance of the sonographically observed changes remains to be elucidated. Analgesic effects must involve mechanisms other than sensory stimulation. Implications: A full, placebo-controlled trial of MCT is warranted. Longer treatment and combination with an exercise programme may enhance its effectiveness; longer-term follow-up is needed to assess recurrence rates. Sonography may help predict treatment response.

title: Treadmill exercise improves memory function after cerebral infarction in rats
abstract: Purpose: The purpose of this study was to investigate the effects of treadmill exercise on memory function after cerebral infarction in rats. Relevance: This study provides a basic evidence for the rehabilitative therapy of memory functional recovery following onset of stroke. Participants: Eight male Wistar rats (200-300 g, 7 weeks old) were used. Methods: Under chloral hydrate anesthesia, animals were subjected to middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO). A nylon monofilament with rounded tip was inserted into the left internal carotid artery and advanced 20mm past the carotid bifurcation until a slight resistance was felt, blocking the MCA at its origin. The filament was left in the place for 90 minutes and then withdrawn. One day after the surgery, sustained hemiparesis was confirmed with neurological deficits and ladder test. Rats with sustained hemiparesis were randomly assigned to two groups: treadmill-exercised group (n = 3) or non-exercised controls (n = 5). From the fourth day after surgery, the rats in the exercise group were forced to run on a motorized treadmill (9 meter/minute) for 30 minutes once a day for 4 weeks. Memory function was examined during the last 5 days of experiment (days 27-32 after MCAO) by three tasks: an object recognition task, an object location task and a passive avoidance task. To control for the effects of motor paralysis on memory evaluation, locomotor activity was measured with an open-field test on the first day of memory assessment. After the last test, rats ware sacrificed under deep anesthesia followed by 2, 3, 5- triphenyltetrazolium chloride (TTC) staining to determine infarct volume. Analysis: Student's t-test was used to compare exercised groups and control. Results: Memory function of the exercised group was significantly improved compared with control, such as the increased time to explore a novel object in the object recognition task (64.2±1.1% and 54.0±2.1%; p < 0.05), location recognition task (62.6±1.6% and 50.9±2.0%; p < 0.05) and the latency to enter the dark compartment in the passive avoidance task (300±0 seconds and 99±51 seconds; p = 0.0858). Motor activity evaluated by an open field test and infarct volume showed no difference between groups. Conclusions: Treadmill exercise demonstrates potential to improve functional memory recovery following transient MCA occlusion in rats without a concomitant increase in motor activity. Implications: These data suggest the possibility that treadmill exercise aids in the recovery from memory deficits post stroke.

title: Video based gait analysis; Essential for modern physiotherapy practice
abstract: Purpose: In the past decades instrumented gait analysis (3-dimensional kinematics, kinetics and electromyography (EMG)) mainly has been used for scientific research. In the late eighties clinicians like Jim Gage and David Sutherland started to use these techniques to inform clinical decision making on surgical interventions in children. Objective kinematics derived by optoelectronic motion capture equipment was used to compare the movements to normal gait. In addition pathological muscle function was quantified using joint kinetics and surface EMG. This enabled the analysis of pathological movement in terms of aetiology to provide a rationale for treatment, i.e. no longer phenomenological. Nowadays the use of this so-called clinical gait analysis has gained clinical acceptance and is used for different gait related problems in both children and adults. However, a major disadvantage is the cost and complexity of the equipment involved. Exploiting a gait laboratory is expensive and often special staff is required for maintenance and data analysis. Fortunately, current developments of multimedia technology enabled the development of “video based gait analysis” at considerable less costs, within reach of the physiotherapy. Specifically a special computer application, the “MoXieviewer”, was developed to analyse the kinematics together with the kinetics and EMG measured. It is made available as freeware on the Internet (www.smalll.nl). Relevance: Knowledge on normal movements is indispensable in order to understand the abnormalities exposed by different patients. Diagnosing the exact abnormalities is essential for correct clinical decision making. Normally the physiotherapist uses clinical examination for this purpose. Video based gait analysis combines the observation of gait together with information on muscle activation patterns (EMG) and ground reaction forces (kinetics). Description: Video based gait analysis is based on the instrumented gait analysis used in clinical gait laboratories throughout the world. Clinical practice showed that the use of split screen video (i.e. the sagittal and frontal views) in most cases is accurate enough to analyse the abnormalities observed. The software to analyse the digital videos (MoXieViewer) was specifically designed to be used in clinical physiotherapy practise. This approach offers the possibility to analyse data without actual presence of the patient and discuss the results with colleagues. During the last decade it has proven its added value in diagnosing gait related problems in for example CP-children, polio, stroke and amputee patients. Evaluation: Video based gait analysis together with the use of the MoXieviewer has been evaluated in different clinical gait laboratories in the Netherlands and nowadays is used in routine clinical decision making. Conclusions: Video based gait analysis has proven its added value in clinical practice in hospitals and rehabilitation centres. The dramatic drop in costs of the recently developed instruments together with the use of the MoXieviewer offers the possibility for physiotherapists to make a big step forward in diagnosing the causes of gait related problems. Implications: Information on possible causes of the patients' complaints normally is gathered by applying clinical tests. Use of video-based clinical gait analysis offers the possibility to make treatment aetiology oriented and gather information on body structures during functional tasks.

title: Development and use of the southampton motor functional indicator (SMFI) as a motor outcome measure in acute paediatric neurological rehabilitation
abstract: Purpose: To devise a simple scoring system to quantify rate of reduction of therapist dependency, in a severely affected acute neurological rehabilitation population, prior to patients scoring on other motor outcome scales. To standardise patient assessment and facilitate treatment/discharge planning. To justify staffing provision and service funding. Relevance: There is no published motor scoring system sensitive to early change in motor abilities for severely impaired patients receiving rehabilitation following acute neurological insult. Southampton University Hospital NHS Trust (SUHT) Paediatric Physiotherapy department developed a simple scoring system to achieve the above aims-the SMFI. SMFI can be applied to all rehabilitation patients, greater than 2 years of age and is not condition specific. It enables therapists to; use SMFI as a prognostic indicator; compare outcome of different conditions; evaluate specific pathology outcomes and justify clinical staffing requirements. The SMFI enables a patients progress to be charted over time, and facilitate those showing prolonged low SMFI scores to have timely discharge planning preventing delayed discharge. Description: The SMFI scores, between 0 and 15, describing patients dependency on therapists undertaking three functional tasks of head/trunk control, standing, and gait. Tasks score 0 (full assistance of multiple therapists required), up to 5 (task performed independently). The SUHT paediatric physiotherapists have utilised the SMFI as a standard objective measure alongside other motor outcome measures encompassing higher level functioning, for all children admitted for acute neurological rehabilitation on initial assessment, at regular intervals and at discharge. Evaluation: 2009-2010 data 40 patients, 19 males: 21 females with median age of 11.5 years (range 2-16), required acute neuro-rehabilitation. 100% patients prospectively scored using SMFI, including 6 stroke, 12 traumatic brain injury, 5 Guillain-Barre Syndrome, 4 neuro-surgery, 5 encephalitis. SMFI score on initial assessment median 1 (range 0-11), at day 5 median 5 (range 0-14) and on discharge median 14 (range 1-15). 100% patients altered between initial and discharge SMFI score (range 1-15). Wilcoxon signed ranks test showed this improvement to be statistically significant (p = 0.005). Conclusions: SMFI is quick and easy to use within a diverse paediatric acute neurological rehabilitation setting (100% completion rate achieved). It has a low ceiling affect but is responsive in those with severe disability prior to scoring on other outcome scores. Implications: SMFI is a useful adjunct to regularly assess and demonstrate change during rehabilitation for patients with high initial therapist dependency. Those achieving the SMFI ceiling would benefit from use of other motor outcome measures. SMFI scores that show little change over time can be used to identify patients who need prolonged rehabilitation periods and can be used to facilitate service design, plan specialist service referral and ongoing care needs. It can be used in both the adult and paediatric populations (over 2 years) with future work concentrating on tool validation.

title: Limaprost alfadex, a prostaglandin E1 derivative, prevents deterioration of forced exercise capability in rats with chronic compression of the spinal cord
abstract: Study Design.: Basic animal research. Objective.: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy is a common condition among elderly and often treated by surgery. To explore possibility of pharmacologic treatment, limaprost alfadex, a prostaglandin E1 derivative with vasodilatory and antiplatelet action, was tried in a rat chronic spinal cord compression model. Summary of Background Data.: Limaprost increased the blood flow of cauda equina and improved motor functions in animal models of lumbar stenosis. The drug is clinically used to treat neurogenic intermittent claudication. METHODS: Forty-two rats were allocated to four groups: (A) sham operation without permanent cord compression, given 5 mL/kg of distilled water twice a day (n = 6); (B) sham operation, receiving 300 μg/kg limaprost twice a day (n = 6); (C) cord compression, receiving the vehicle (n = 15); and (D) cord compression receiving the drug (n = 15). A thin polyurethane sheet that expands by absorbing water was implanted under the C5-C6 laminae to produce cord compression. For sham operation, the sheet was immediately removed. Exercise tests were repeated on a rotating treadmill until 26 weeks after surgery, and then the animals were killed and the spinal cord harvested for motor neurons counts. Results.: Treadmill endurance (seconds, mean ± standard error of mean) 2 weeks after surgery was 497.7 ± 2.3, 434.5 ± 65.5, 423.1 ± 33.0, and 480.5 ± 19.5 in groups A, B, C, and D, respectively. At 26th week, the duration was 497.7 ± 2.3, 421.2 ± 78.8, 21.3 ± 11.7, and 441.3 ± 40.4 (P < 0.0001 for the decrease in C group, multivariate analysis of variance with correction for multiple measures.) The motor neuron counts were 38.3 ± 3.6, 38.2 ± 2.6, 32.6 ± 1.9, and 36.2 ± 2.3 in groups A, B, C, and D (P = 0.34), respectively. Conclusion.: Limaprost alfadex prevented decline of forced locomotion capability in rats with chronic compression of the cervical cord. Copyright © 2011 Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

title: Benefits of Exercise Therapy in Peripheral Arterial Disease
abstract: Peripheral arterial disease (PAD) is a common disorder caused largely by atherosclerosis. Although it is associated with increased morbidity and cardiovascular mortality, PAD remains underdiagnosed. Traditional PAD care has involved cardiovascular risk factor modification, use of antiplatelet agents, and revascularization. For those individuals who are eligible and willing to perform exercise therapy (ET), a significant benefit may be recognized. Despite this, ET faces several challenges to implementation. Notably, the lack of reimbursement by third party payers remains the major challenge to routine use of ET. © 2011 Elsevier Inc.

title: Shunt surgery in patients with hydrocephalus and white matter changes: Clinical article
abstract: Object. Patients with idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH) often present with impaired gait and cognition together with ventricular enlargement and normal intracranial pressure. Many have vascular risk factors as well as periventricular and deep white matter changes on MR imaging. Abnormal CSF dynamics, that is, high resistance to outflow or improvement after CSF drainage, indicate good effects of shunt surgery. The authors examined whether the worst-case iNPH patients with extensive vascular white matter disease and normal CSF dynamics would benefit from shunt surgery. These patients also fulfilled the criteria for Binswanger disease. Therefore, a randomized controlled double-blind study was performed. Methods. Fourteen consecutive patients fulfilling the above criteria were randomized to receive either open or closed shunts. At 3 months after surgery, the patients with initially ligated shunts had their shunts opened. Clinical evaluation consisting of 7 quantitative psychometric and 6 continuous gait tests was performed preoperatively and 3 and 6 months after surgery. Results. Patients randomized to receive open shunts had improved motor (30% increase) and psychometric (23% increase) scores 3 months after shunt placement. There were no significant changes between the 3- and 6-month follow-up in these same patients. Conversely, those with initially ligated shunts were unchanged during the first 3-month period, although they improved in both motor (28%) and cognitive (18%) functions following removal of the ligature. Conclusions. Patients with enlarged ventricles, hydrocephalic symptoms, and extensive vascular white matter changes benefit from shunt surgery. ©1944-2011 by the American Association of Neurosurgeons.

title: Cardiac rehabilitation outcome following percutaneous coronary intervention compared to cardiac surgery
abstract: To examine differences in objective and subjective outcomes in outpatients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) performed for acute myocardial infarction versus cardiac surgery (CS) following a phase II cardiac rehabilitation (CR). Longitudinal observational study of 437 consecutive cardiac outpatients after 8 weeks of phase II CR. Patients were divided into the PCI group (n = 281) and CS group (n = 156). Handgrip and knee extensor muscle strength, peak oxygen uptake (VO2), upper- and lower-body self-efficacy for physical activity (SEPA), and physical component summary (PCS) and mental component summary (MCS) scores as assessed by Short Form-36 were measured at 1 and 3 months after PCI or CS. All outcomes increased significantly between months 1 and 3 in both groups. However, increases were greater in the CS versus PCI group in handgrip strength (+12.3 % vs. +8.1%, P < 0.01), knee extensor muscle strength (+19.3% vs. +17.5%, P = 0.008), peak VO2 (+20.9% vs. +16.9%, P < 0.01), upper-body SEPA (+27.7% vs. +9.2%, P = 0.001), and PCS score (+6.5% vs. +4.1%, P = 0.001). Although this relatively short-term phase II CR increased all outcomes for both groups, outcomes showed the recovery process was different between the PCI and CS groups, slightly favoring CS patients. Furthermore, patents in the field of CR are presented. © 2011 Bentham Science Publishers.

title: Exercise stress echo in asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis with low gradient and preserved left ventricular function
abstract: Background: According to recent publications asymptomatic low gradient severe aortic stenosis with preserved left ventricular function (low A-S) is a group of patients (pts) with similar baseline characteristics and probably different prognosis, compared to high gradient ones (high A-S). However, there are no studies addressing the exercise response in this group. Hence we sought to compare the findings in low A-S and high A-S pts undergoing exercise stress echo (ESE). Methods: We evaluated the cardiac Doppler and ergometric parameters of all asymptomatic pts with severe aortic stenosis (valvular area < 1 cm2) and preserved left ventricular function (ejection fraction > 50%) who underwent ESE in one institution from 2002 to 2010. We considered two groups: A (aortic mean gradient > 40 mmHg) and B (< 40 mmHg) at baseline Doppler. After maximal ESE, we compared the findings between both groups. Exclusion criteria were moderate or severe aortic/mitral regurgitation (6 pts), baseline motion abnormalities (32 pts) and presence of atrial fibrillation (1 pt). Results: One hundred and ninety four pts were included (Group A: 147; B: 47 pts). There were no differences between groups at baseline in age (A: 66,8±14.5 y; B: 65±14.4 y, p=ns); sex male (A: 49,3%; B: 61%, p=ns); heart rate (A: 70±13.8 bpm; B: 71±12.9 bpm, p=ns); systolic blood pressure (A: 126±18.9 mmHg; B: 129±21 mmHg, p=ns); wall motion index (WMI): 1 in both groups (p=ns), ejection fraction, 59,5% in A group vs 60,9% in B group (p=ns), previous hypertension (A: 75,7%; B: 65,4%, p=ns), type 2 diabetes (A: 12,9%; B: 19,1%, p=ns); previous coronary angioplasty (A: 5,7%; B: 4,4%, p=ns); coronary surgical revascularization (A: 2,9%; B: 1,5%, p=ns). There were no differences in METS achieved (A: 6.7±3; B: 6,6±3,5, p=ns), and heart rate at maximal stress (A:128±26 bpm; B: 123±36 bpm, p=ns). Group A pts received less medical treatment (5,7% vs 16,9%, p= 0,024) than B Group, while aortic valve area was smaller in Group A (0,61 ±0.15cm2 vs 0,77±0.15 cm2 in Group B, p=0.001). At maximal exercise stress ejection fraction was lower in Group A (55,8%) compared to Group B (61,9%), p= 0,02. WMI was higher in Group A (1,09±0.24 vs 1,03±0.09, p= 0,04), and stroke work loss index was higher in Group A (31,6±6.6 vs 19,3±4.6 in B Group,p= 0,001). Systolic blood pressure fall > 20 mmHg on exercise occurred in 8,8% of Group A pts and none of Group B (p= 0,01). Conclusion: Pts with low A-S have a better response under maximal exercise stress compared with high A-S pts. These findings relates with larger aortic valve areas and lower WMI at maximal stress, that could be expression of an earlier stage of the disease.

title: Impaired Right ventricular longitudinal function causes lower exercise capacity in patients after myocardial infarction
abstract: Background: Right ventricular (RV) dysfunction is common in patients after myocardial infarction (MI). RV longitudinal function plays most important role in RV kinesis. In patients with chronic heart failure RV dysfunction causes worsening of exercise capacity (EC) and is independent parameter of worse prognosis. Data on impact of RV function on EC in patients after myocardial infarction (MI) with preserved left ventricle (LV) ejection fraction (EF) are scarce. Aim: To assess EC in patients with RV dysfunction complicating inferior MI in comparison to patients without RV dysfunction. Methods: We evaluated prospectively patients with first inferior MI with ST segment elevation treated by primary percutaneous coronary intervention (pPCI) and preserved or mildly impaired LV systolic function (LV EF ≥ 45%). ECHO was performed post pPCI within 48 hours from the onset of symptoms. According to the Guidelines for the Echocardiographic Assessment of the Right Heart in Adults, RV dysfunction estimated with Tissue Doppler Echocardiography (TDE) was defined as Sm RV < 10 cm/s at the basal segment of RV free wall. Cardiopulmonary Exercise Test (CPET) was done on day 14 ±10. V02 peak and V02-AT and percent of predicted values (%) were assessed as EC parameters. None of the patients had exercise limiting factors other than dyspnoe and/or fatigue. Results: Patients (n=90, 75,5% males, mean age 60,5±10 years) were divided into two groups: the group with RV systolic dysfunction (n=32, 78% males, mean age 61,1± 8,9 years) and the group without RV systolic dysfunction (n=58, 74% males, mean age 60,2±10,9 years). RV dysfunction was assessed regardless of electrocardiographically diagnosed RV MI. The group with RV dysfunction has a significant lower EC measured as percent of predicted values of VO2 max (comparison of EC parameters is shown in the table). No significant differences in LV diastolic function assessed as peak early diastolic velocity (Em LV) was noticed between groups with and without RV systolic dysfunction (7,4±2,9 vs 7,9±2,7 cm/s P=NS). According to multivariate regression analysis, LV systolic parameters as LV EF and wall motion score index (WMSI) had no impact on EC. (Table presented) Conclusion: RV longitudinal systolic function in patients after acute inferior MI predicts exercise capacity estimated with cardiopulmonary stress test.

title: Prevalence and associated health status of frailty in older adults undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention
abstract: Background: Frailty is common in older adults but its association with health status (patients' symptoms, function and quality of life) is unknown. Methods: We prospectively recruited patients ≥65 years (n = 629) who underwent PCI at Mayo Clinic (Rochester, MN) and Franciscan Skemp Hospital (LaCrosse, WI) and survived until hospital discharge (10/2005 to 09/2008) to assess for frailty and health status. Frailty status was determined based on deficits due to weight loss, exhaustion, physical activity, gait speed, and grip strength (≥3 features = frail; 1-2 features = intermediate frailty; 0 features = not frail) and compared with comorbidities and health status [Short-Form 36 (SF-36) and Seattle Angina Questionnaire (SAQ)]. A multivariable linear regression model was used to estimate the association of frailty with health status. Results: Of 629 patients, 117 (19%) were frail, 298 (47%) had intermediate frailty, and 130 were not frail (21%). Incomplete data precluded classification in 84 patients (13%). Frail patients had higher rates than non-frail patients of hypertension, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, heart failure, peripheral arterial disease, prior stroke, and prior myocardial infarction (p <0.05 for each comparison), including more prevalent left main or multivessel disease (p<0.05). Multivariable linear regression adjusting for age, sex, and comorbid illnesses demonstrated poorer health status in PCI-treated patients with any frailty (Figure). Frail patients reported lower general (SF-36) and disease-specific (SAQ) health status than non-frail patients, with estimated effect sizes 1.8 to 8.8 times greater than the impact of a 10-year increase in age. Conclusions: One-fifth of older patients referred for PCI are frail and frailty is associated with greater comorbidity and poorer health status. Frailty may add a new dimension to risk prediction in the elderly and its assessment should be incorporated into risk stratification. Graph Presented.

title: Coronary intervention through transradial access in the very elderly: Results and comparison to the elderly
abstract: Background: Transradial approach (TA) to coronary interventions (PCI) is an effective alternative to femoral approach in patients (p) >70 years old (Elderly) due to fewer vascular complications and improved comfort. We aim to assess the efficacy, safety and comfort of the TA for PCI in p>80 years old (Very Elderly) and to compare the results with TA PCI in 70-79 years old p. Methods: We analyzed 100 consecutive TA PCI p>80 years old (Group A) and we compared them with 100 consecutive TA PCI p 70- 79 years old (Group B). Exclusions: p with mild or absent radial pulse, (-) Allen test, primary PCI or in shock. We analyzed feasibility of TA (PCI completed through TA), MACE (death, AMI, emergency PCI or CABG, stroke); TA procedural success (residual stenosis <20% without MACE), mayor vascular complications (bleeding requiring prolonged hospitalization, surgery or transfusion; pseudoaneurysm; arteriovenous fistula; limb ischemia; nerve damage); and minor vascular complications (haematoma, neuritis). We assessed comfort considering 5 items: overall discomfort, access site pain, ability to walk, difficulty to urinate, low back pain. We applied a 0-2 scale PCI-specific questions with a lower value indicating better comfort. Results: Compared to 70-79 years old p we found more Severe Vascular Tortuosity in the Very Elderly, and more p required the use Wholey® or Hydrophilic 0.035 wires for overcoming the difficulty. See TABLE. Conclusions: TA for PCI in the Very Elderly is feasible, effective, safe and comfortable. We found more vascular tortuosity than in 70-79 years old p. The TA for PCI results technically more challenging in the Very Elderly as compared to the Elderly, without affecting feasibility, effectiveness, safeness or comfort (Table Presented).

title: MLC 901 (Neuroaid10), a traditional chinese medicine protects the brain against global ischemia in rats
abstract: Background: Global ischemia leads to neuronal damage in the vulnerable hippocampal CA1 field and to deficits in motor and cognitive functions. Today mild hypothermia remains the only therapy for human patients. The need for new therapeutic strategies is imperative. NeuroAid (MLC601 and MLC901), a Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) which is used in China to facilitate recovery of patients after stroke has been described in a model of focal ischemia as a protective drug with neurogenerative and neuroproliferative properties. The aim of this work was to investigate the therapeutic efficacy of MLC901 on brain injury and motor deficits induced by ischemia. Methods: Ischemia was induced by4-vessel occlusion for 20 min. MLC901 (Moleac) was administered by 1 i.p. injection at the concentration of 74, 7.4, 0.74 or 0.074 mg/ml 30 min, 1, 2 or 3 hours after ischemia followed by one injection/day after reperfusion. Motor and cognitive performances were tested by the grip test and the Morris water maze (MWM),. The neuronal damage was assessed. Results: Ischemia resulted in degeneration of CA1 neurons. MLC901 (0.074mg/ml) prevented necrosis and apoptosis of neurons up to 3 hours after ischemia. MLC901 led to a decrease in Bax expression and MDA levels induced by the ischemia. We demonstrated the critical role of Akt pathway in the MLC901-mediated neuroprotection against CA1 brain injury. MLC901 enhanced the neurogenesis and stimulated BDNF expression. MLC901 induced an improvement of the strength force. In the MWM, when compared to ischemic rats, MLC901 reduced the escape latency and swim distance and increased the time spent in the plateform quadrant. Conclusion: This work demonstrates that MLC901 can offer a potent protection against global ischemia-induced brain injury with resulting preservation of learning and memory abilities. MLC901 can represent a novel therapeutic strategy after cardiac arrest or coronary surgery with a time-window of protection clinically interesting.

title: Diffusion weighted MRI and pyramidal tract damage as prognostic marker for functional outcome after spinal cord infarction
abstract: Background: The pathogenesis, magnetic resonance imaging findings and the prognosis of spontaneous non-surgical spinal ischemia remain mostly unexplored. Our purpose is to phenotype spinal ischemia with clinical MR-tomographic and electrophysiological criteria to determine criteria for outcome and comparison to existing literature. Methods: We analyzed prospectively the data from our stroke registry of patients suffering from vascular spinal cord ischemia from 2004 to 2010. Cases that were due to aortic surgery, compressive, tumoral or inflammatory pathologies were excluded. We analyzed the clinical, neurophysiological, imaging and functional outcome data for 10 patients with acute spinal cord infarction admitted to our comprehensive stroke center. Outcome was evaluated at the end of rehabilitation. Results: Mean age was 71 (age range 50-84 years; 5 women). 7 patients showed damage of lower thoracic spinal cord (T8-L5) and 3 patients with upper thoracic/cervical damage (C4-T6). In 5 patients etiology remained cryptogenic, other etiologies were cardiac embolism, systemic atherosclerosis (myelomalacia), thrombophilia, and post-radiation. After rehabilitation 4 patients had regained full walking ability or were able to walk with aids and 6 were wheelchair bound. Spinal diffusion weighted MRI were pathological in 8/10 patients during the first week. All patients with unfavorable outcome (no walking ability) showed severe pyramidal tract lesion by performing motor evoked potentials in combination with DWI abnormalities of the spinal cord during the first week. Conclusion: Poor outcome was associated with severe electrophysiological changes and DWI hyperintensities on the MRI. Patients with a favorable outcome had either no DWI hyperintensities or either normal/mild electrophysiological changes.

title: A comparison of door-to-balloon time at an urban ST elevation myocardial infarction (stemi) receiving center: Walk-in versus paramedic arrival
abstract: Background: With the advent of STEMI receiving centers (SRCs) more patients are triaged in the field and preferentially transported to hospitals capable of primary percutaneous coronary intervention. SRCs have reduced delays in angioplasty, but they have also highlighted disparities in door-to-balloon time between STEMI patients who present as walk-ins versus those who are identified in the field and arrive via paramedics. Objectives: To compare door-to-balloon time between patients identified in the field as having a STEMI and transported to a SRC and patients who walked in to the emergency department (ED) of a SRC with a STEMI. Methods: Data were collected prospectively on all STEMI patients who presented to the ED from January 2009 through September 2010. Two groups of patients were compared: patients identified as a STEMI in the field and brought in by paramedics after calling 9-1-1, and those who walked in. The time from arrival in the ED to successful balloon angioplasty was compared, as were interval times between each discrete step: a) door to ECG b) ECG to activation c) activation to team arrival d) team arrival to patient arrival in cardiac cath lab e) patient in lab to attending arrival in cardiac cath lab and f) attending arrival to successful balloon angioplasty. The Wilcoxon rank-sum test was used to compare the mean times between the two groups. Results: The study included a total of 295 STEMI patients: 161 patients transported by paramedics to the SRC and 134 walk-in patients. The overall door-to-balloon time for the paramedic transport group was 60 minutes and for the walk-in group 136 minutes (p<0.0001); 90% of paramedic transport patients versus 53% of walk-in patients had door-to-balloon time £ 90 minutes (p<0.0001). Walk-in patients had significantly longer mean door to ECG time (49 min vs. 8 min p<0.0001), mean ECG to activation time (44 min vs. 5 min p<0.0001), and patient arrival in lab to attending arrival in lab time (12 min vs. 10 min p=0.0063). Conclusion: STEMI patients transported to a SRC by paramedics more frequently received angioplasty in less than 90 minutes in comparison to walk-in STEMI patients. Specific areas of delay were identified and additional investigation is needed for improvement of door-to-balloon time for walk-in patients.

title: Effects of exercise training on functional capacity and quality of life in heart failure patients
abstract: Aim: People with heart failure can experience marked reductions in their activities of daily living and health-related quality of life (QOL) because of their restricted heart capacity. Exercise training programmes improved health-related QOL compared to usual care without the exercise. Because that, the aim of this study was to evaluate the impact of supervised short-term exercise training on functional capacity and QOL in patients with chronic heart failure (CHF). Methods: The study included 72 patients of both sexes (46 males and 26 females), mean age 63.5 ± 6.3 years, EF 36.6 ± 9.2%, who were sent for treatment and rehabilitation after myocardial infarction and revascularization procedures. Patients were included in the 3-week rehabilitation program, based on a strictly controlled and individual prescribed physical training. Before and after rehabilitation, all patients underwent exercise stress test, by Naughton tredmill exercise protocol. Quality of life was assessed by filling the questionnaire Minnesota Living With Heart Failure Questionnaire (MLWHF). Results: After of short-term exercise training, recorded a significant increase in the level of exercise tolerance, (p < 0,005) duration of exercise testing (p < 0,005) and significantly reduce the rate-pressure product at rest (p < 0,005) while the rate-pressure product at the end of the test was higher after the trainings (p < 0,01). All three dimension of the MLWHF questionnaire were significantly improved (reduced) after 3-weeks exercise training; total score (p = 0,001), physical dimension (p = 0,004) and emotional dimension (p = 0,001). Conclusion: The short-time exercise training increased functional capacity, decreased symptoms and improved QOL in heart failure patients.

title: Percutaneous, intra-myocardial injection of unselected bone marrow-derived mononuclear cells via NOGA-XP significantly improves ejection fraction in post-infarct patients: ALSTER Stem Cell
abstract: Aims: Here we describe the results of the single-center, prospective, controlled, open-label ALSTER-Stem Cell trial. Methods and results: The trial recruited 10 patients following acute myocardial infarction (CKmax 2667±575 U/l) and succesful revascularisation fulfilling die following inclusion criteria: EF was <45% and NT-proBNP elevated 3x norm (1822±443pg/ml) measured 10-15days after revascularisation by cardiac MRI and echocardiography; patients presented with NYHA>=II at the time of screening. The initial infarct was due to occlusion of the proximal LAD in 6 patients; 4 patients presented with RCA occlusion. These strict inclusion criteria lead to slow recrution for the trial but a specific subset of infarct patients, namely young patients with late reperfusion: patients aged 54.9±3.6 years with timing of symptoms to hospital admission (6 hours up to 48 h); revascularisation was performed within 2 h of hospital admission. A diameter of the ventricular wall of less than 6 mm or a ventricular thrombus at the time of screening were contraindications for inclusion. Patients with contraindications giving infonned consent were included in the control group presenting otherwise with similar characteristics; this cohort consists of four patients. 3 days after revascularisation patients were subjected to injection of autologous mononuclear cells employing the MYOSTAR injection catheter following dcctroanatornical LV mapping via the NOGA-XP system. Cells were injected into the infarct borderzone defined by a unipolar activity between 6 and 12 mV. The patients received in total 129.9±13 × 10(6) cells by 15-20 injections. Treated patients and control patients received cardiac MRI and NT-proBNP measurements as well as 6min walk test and echocardiography at baseline (10-20 days after revascularisation) and 6 months; with the exemption of cardiac MRI, all parameters were also obtained at one year. Global ejection fraction as measured by short axis cardiac MRI improved by 7.9 ±1.9% (p=0.003) at 6 months compared to baseline calculated intra-individually. 6min walk distance also improved significantiy (baseline vs. FU 66±20.5m at 6 months) as well as echocardiographic parameters of diastolic dysfunction (VE/VE': -4.0±1.4, p=0.01 baseline vs. 6month FU). NT-proBNP improved significantiy (-1019± 280 pg/ ml, p=0.006 baseline vs. 6 months). No patient died or had other adverse cardiac events including repeat revascularisation or rhythm abnormalities. In contrast, control patients did not improve their ejection fraction (+0.4 ±0 2%) over 6 months as measured by cardiac MRI. Conclusions: Patients with reduced ejection fraction following acute myocardial infarction can be safely and efficiently treated with intra-myocardial injection of concentrated bone marrow cells. The expected LV remodeling following large infarcts was prevented. The trial is too small to draw definite conclusions: nevertheless the data support the hypothesis that intra-myocardial cell therapy following acute infarct may be a suitable therapeutic strategy and warrants further large studies.

title: Coronary atherosclerotic disease in Saudi patients: A pilot intravascular ultrasound analytical study of patients presenting with Acute Coronary Syndrome
abstract: Aims: Our study is designed to investigate the spectrum of Coronary Adiero-Thrombosis (CAT) of our Saudi patients(pts) with very high prevalence of Diabetes presenting with Acute Coronary Syndromes (ACS). Methods and results: At Prince Salman Heart Center/King Fahad Medical City, total of 60 pts Intra-Vascular Ultrasound (IVUS) studies were retrospectively reviewed, 105 IVUS runs studied, of whom 38(35 pts) were carried out for Borderline Lesions Pre-Runs (PR) and 67(25 pts) were carried out for post stent deployment(PS). We report our first 35 consecutive pts who had IVUS for evaluating their borderline lesions. Each run was divided into 1mm slices, each of which required 2 separate Luminal and External Elastic Membrane (EEM) tracings, lesions within 5 mm Proximal and Distal to the maximal Plaque Burden(PB) were analysed. The following parameters were obtained(mean±SD): Average Luminal Diameter(ALD): The (average of Minimal Luminal Diameter and Maximal Luminal Diameter). Luminal Area (LA): The External Elastic Membrane (EEM) Cross Sectional Area (CSA) of the vessel lumen. Average Vessel Diameter (AVD): The average of all vessel EEM diameters obtained from each slice. Vessel Area (VA): The CSA of the vessel wall using EEM of each slice. Plaque Area (PA): The EEM CSA - Lumen CSA. Plaque Burden (PB): The Plaque CSA / EEM CSA. Remodelling Index(RMI): The EEM CSA Lesion / EEM CSA of the average Proximal and Distal Reference Vessel (RV): Obtained from the most normal looking segments with the least PB 5mm Proximal and Distal to the Lesion 1. EEM Volume: the sum (Σ) EEM CSA Lumen Volume: The sum (Σ) Lumen CSA Plaque Volume: The sum (Σ) (EEM CSA - Lumen CSA) Percent Plaque Volume: The [Σ] (EEM CSA - Lumen CSA / EEM CSA) x 100- Twenty eight Males (80%) and 7 Females (20%), average age 55 years. Twenty seven pts were diabetics (DM) (77.14%) and 8 were non-diabetics (NDM) (22.86%), 14 pts were smokers & ex-smokers (40%). Pts were admitted for ACS including, 12 pts (34.29%) with recent ST segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI), 8 pts (22.86%) with Non-STEMI (NSTEMI), and 5 pts (42.85%) with Unstable Angina (UA). Nine pts had no f7u Cardiac Troponin-I(CT-I) of whom 4 had baseline CT-I levels. Five pts had no baseline CT-I levels (30 pts were analysed). CT-I was positive in 19 (54.29%) of whom 8 pts with STEMI (42.11%), 7 pts with NSTEMI (36.84%) and 4 pts with UA (21.05%). Conclusions: This IVUS pilot study is the first of its kind imaging and tissue characterising of CAT in Saudi patients with very high prevelance of DM presenting with ACS. The findings in diabetics are significantly smaller L D (p=0.0497) much smaller V D(p=0.0080), VA (p=0.0088) and PA(p=0.02) compared to NDM. These findings were much more prevelant in pts presenting with Acute STEMI, and NSTEMI but not in pts presenting with UA. Larger PB was associated with acute swelling and plaque rupture within severe, diffusely diseased coronaries and predominandy in diabetics that are likely to be unique to our population.

title: Prospective, randomized trial on surgical treatment of grade III hemorrhoids: Hemorrhoidectomy versus doppler-guided transanal hemorrhoidal dearterialization and anopexy
abstract: Purpose: Transanal hemorrhoidal dearterialization is a new approach for patients with hemorrhoidal disease that reduces vascular flow to the anal cushions, however it may fail for advanced haemorrhoids due to persistent prolapse. In this study we compared short term results of excisional hemorrhoidectomy and transanal hemorrhoidal dearterialization coupled with an anopexy, which restores the prolapsed mucosa into the anal canal, in patients with grade III hemorrhoids Methods: Between August and October 2010, 30 consecutive patients (12 male), mean age 58, with grade III haemorrhoids, were randomly assigned to hemorrhoidectomy (MM, Group 1) and doppler-guided transanal dearterialization and anopexy (THD, Group 2). Pre- and postoperative symptoms, operative time, complications, return to daily activity and personal satisfaction were recorded. Pain was evaluated by means of a VAS scale, symptoms by a questionnaire filled on day 1 to 7, 14 and 30. Statistical analysis was performed by student-t test for continuous variable, chi-square for dichotomous and ordinal variable, non parametric test were indicated Results: 16 patients underwent MM and 14 THD operations. Mean operative time was 34 min for group 1 and 38 for group 2 (p= ns). During THD procedure 6 six arteries were ligated in all patients and 3-4 running sutures were performed above the dentate line in order to lift the prolapse. No serious complications were reported in both groups. Mean VAS at day 1, 7, 14, 30 were 8 vs 4, 5 vs 2, 4 vs 0 and 2 vs 0 in group 1 and 2 respectively. No patients suffered from persistent bleeding at one month, one patient in group 2 experienced persistence of single pile prolapse, one in group 1 developped an anal fissure that was treated by topical nitrate. Daily or working activity was fully restarted after 13 and 7 days on average Conclusions: Hemorrhoidal dearterialization and anopexy showed similar postoperative morbidity and effectiveness as excisional hemorrhoidectomy with minimal postoperative pain, early return of patients to their normal activities and increased patients' satisfaction.

title: Using the paclitaxel-coated balloon in treating of in-stent restenosis
abstract: Objective: Drug eluting balloons could offer a viable alternative to drug eluting stents (DES) in the treatment of coronary artery disease. The balloon technology concept is that paclitaxel would be more evenly distributed along the vessel wall compared with being eluted from stent struts. Methods: The study included 90 endovascular interventions performed from 2007 to 2010 for the treatment of in-stent restenosis (ISR). The patients were classified into two equal groups based on an endovascular technique used. Patients of group I (n=35) were managed using a coronary balloon catheter coated with paclitaxel (Dior, BBraun). ISR in group II (n=55) were revasculated with standard balloon angioplasty. Patients developed ISR and required the repeated revascularization in 9.64±4.7 months after primary stent implantation. Angina pectoris II-III (angina upon exertion II-III) presented in 26 (74%) patients in group I and 41 (74.6%) patients in groups II. Intercurrent DM was diagnosed in three (9%) patients and six (11%) patients of the respective groups. The length of stented segments varied from 12 to 114 (31.4±18.2) mm in group I, and from eight to 110 (32.4±21.4) mm in group II. The ISR severity has been estimated with digital angiography as 82.6±11.6% and 74±11.6% of the respective groups. PTCA of the repeat lesions was performed in all cases. Patients in group I were treated with PTCA using a standard balloon with the mean length=26.9±5.7 mm. PTCA in group II was performed with paclitaxelcoated technique with the mean length of the balloon=23.7±5.7 mm. The residual stenosis was <10% in all groups. Results: Long-term outcome after angioplasty was assessed in 18 (51.4) and 24 (43.6%) patients of the divided groups. The digital angiography was repeated within 6.4±1.1 months. Angiographic restenosis was revealed in four (22.2%) cases in group I and in 13 (54.2%) cases in group II (P<0.05). Conclusions: Paclitaxel balloon coating is safe, it effectively inhibits restenosis after coronary angioplasty.

title: Long-term results of an aortobifemoral reconstruction in patients with severe femoral artery calcinosis
abstract: Objective: The results of lower limb revascularization in patients with severe calcinosis of peripheral arteries are controversial and not fully illuminated in available literature (Allota et al. 2004; Lockhart et al. 2004). The goal of our research work was to assess the impact of femoral artery calcinosis (FAC) on the long-term outcomes following aortofemoral bypass (AFB) surgery. Methods: From 2004 to 2009, 209 patients with atherosclerotic lesions of the terminal aorta and iliac arteries have been consecutively treated using bifurcated PTFE vascular grafts. Men predominated in study population (91.9%). Age median of treated subjects was 66.9±6.7 years. Indications for surgical intervention included aorto-iliac occlusive disease with grade II (35.4%), III (50.2%) and IV (14.4%) chronic limb ischemia according to R. Fontaine. One-third of operated subjects underwent profundaplasty in order to improve distal run-off. Long-term follow-up was available in 61 patients. Twenty-six patients were diagnosed to have severe FAC. Other 35 subjects were present without objective signs of FAC. Primary patency, limb salvage and survival rates were assessed in these two groups by using Kaplan-Meier analysis. Patency of vascular graft was determined by duplex ultrasound imaging according to the guidelines by Rutherford et al. (1997). A log-rank and χ2-tests were used to compare obtained results. Results: Both groups were similar with regard to age, sex, race, prevalence of diabetes mellitus and other risk factors for atherosclerosis, indications for surgery, duration of peripheral atherosclerosis occlusive disease. There were statistically significant differences in a thickness of the left ventricle posterior wall [11.17±1.33 mm vs. 9.91±1.81 mm, (P<0.001)] and thickness of the carotid intima-media complex [1.28±0.12 mm vs. 1.24±0.11 mm, (P<0.01)] between two groups. All mentioned parameters were higher in FAC group. Primary patency, foot salvage and survival rates at 60 months period were 52.7%, 59.8%, 64.5% in the FAC group and 85.1%, 87.1%, 71.9% in non-FAC group, respectively (for all comparing variables P<0.01). Conclusions: FAC may influence long-term outcomes following AFB possibly due to increased overall peripheral vascular resistance and rapid progression of atherosclerosis in peripheral and coronary arteries.

title: Do angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors improve walking distance in patients with symptomatic lower limb arterial disease? A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
abstract: Background: Several studies have reported the clinical effects of long-term treatment with cardioprotective medications in patients with lower limb peripheral arterial disease (PAD) in terms of reducing cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. A number of these studies investigated the clinical effect of angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEIs) on walking distance in this group of patients. Objective: To review the evidence regarding the effects of ACEIs in patients with symptomatic PAD of the lower limbs in terms of the effect on maximum and pain-free walking distances and ankle brachial pressure index (ABPI). Methods: A systematic literature search of the medical literature from 1966 to 2010 on randomized placebo-controlled trials which assessed the effect of ACEIs on maximum and/or pain-free walking distances and/or ABPI in patients with symptomatic lower limbs PAD was performed. Data from included studies were pooled with use of random-effects model with standard mean differences. Heterogeneity across studies was assessed with calculation of I2 statistic. Results: From a total of 346 publications identified, 34 articles were selected for full review based on title and abstract. 4 RCTs comprising 576 patients (334(58%) males, mean age 60.7 years, age range (58-66)) met the inclusion criteria and were systematically reviewed. Of those, 137 (24%) patients suffered from symptomatic lower limb PAD. Maximum walking distances were pooled successfully from all 4 studies. After analysing these data, we found significant heterogeneity among the groups and no significant difference in the pooled treatment effect (standard mean difference = 0.46, 95% CI (-0.99-1.92), p = 0.53, I2; = 95%). Pain-free walking distances and ankle brachial pressure indices were pooled successfully from 3 studies and showed an insignificant overall treatment effect (standard mean difference = 0.97, 95% CI (-0.24-2.18), p = 0.12 and 0.68, 95% CI (-0.70-2.06), p = 0.33, respectively). Conclusion: The evidence regarding ACE inhibition efficacy on treadmill walking distance in patients with intermittent claudication is contradicting and lacked properly powered RCTs. However, based on this study, ACEIs did not improve treadmill walking distance and ABPI in patients with symptomatic lower limb arterial disease. Further research from properly powered RCTs is needed. © 2010 Surgical Associates Ltd.

title: C-Cure multicenter trial: Lineage specified bone marrow derived cardiopoietic mesenchymal stem cells for treatment of ischemic cardiomyopathy
abstract: Background: Inter-patient variability in stem cell repair confounds outcome of cardiac regenerative therapies. In preclinical testing, growth factors-guided cardiopoietic specification of human bone marrow derived mesenchymal stem cells (MSC) ensured reparative uniformity. The ensuing multicenter C-Cure clinical trial is designed to assess feasibility and safety of cardiopoietic (CP) MSCs therapy in ischemic heart failure. Methods: Forty-five patients with heart failure of ischemic origin were randomized to standard medical care or autologous CP MSCs (600-1200x106) treatment delivered into viable but dysfunctional left ventricular (LV) segments using electromechanical guidance. All patients were on ICD prophylaxis. Results: Demographic and clinical baseline data were similar between 24 controls and 21 patients treated with CP MSCs. Delivery of CP MSCs was feasible without peri-procedural complications. At cumulative follow up of 7385 days (range from 235 to 564 days, median 334 days), no evidence of cell-induced systemic toxicity or pro-arrhythmogenicity was detected. In 18 patients with arrhythmic events, 63 episodes were detected in controls (2.6/patient) vs 42 episodes in the CP MSCs group (2.0/patient). Five ventricular fibrillation episodes requiring ICD shock were all detected in controls, and none recorded in the CP MSCs group. At 6 months follow-up, clinical performance assessed from the 6 min walk-test improved in CP MSCs treated patients by 52±19 m while it worsened by-21±14 m in controls (p=0.003). While left ventricular end-diastolic volumes decreased to a similar extent, the reduction of the end-systolic volume was 3-fold larger in the CP MSCs treated than control group (-22±4 vs-8±3 mL, p=0.01) and paralleled a significant increase in LV ejection fraction (5.2±0.6% vs 1±0.7%, p<0.0001). Conclusions: The C-Cure study demonstrates the feasibility and safety profile of administering lineage-specified mesenchymal stem cells for cardiac repair in ischemic cardiomyopathy. Efficacy signals related to improvements in left ventricular and clinical performance are consistent with a generalized therapeutic benefit.

title: Peripheral vascular function may be a predictor of exercise performance in Fontan-palliated patients
abstract: Background: Following the Fontan operation, single ventricle patients are at substantial risk for the development of impaired functional status. However, few early markers of suboptimal outcomes have been identified. We sought to determine if low peripheral vascular function might be a marker of altered exercise performance. Methods: Asymptomatic Fontan patients 8-25 years of age were recruited along with age-and sex-matched healthy controls. Endothelial pulse amplitude was measured at baseline and during reactive hyperemia using a non-invasive fingertip peripheral arterial tonometry (PAT) device. Raw data were transformed into the PAT ratio, an established marker of vascular function. Cardiopulmonary exercise testing was performed using the Bruce protocol. Results: Fifty-one Fontan patients (median 15 years [IQR 10.9-17.8]) and 22 controls (15 years [12.5-16.9]) completed testing. Demographics and baseline characteristics were similar between groups. In the Fontan cohort, 94% of patients were NYHA functional class I and 88% had a BNP level <50 pg/mL. Baseline pulse amplitude, a measure that reflects resting arterial tone, was higher in Fontan patients than controls (274 [196-413] vs. 186 [114-279], p=0.03). PAT ratio, a measure of reactive hyperemia, was lower in Fontan patients (0.17 [-0.04-0.44] vs. 0.50 [0.27-0.74], p=0.002). Key parameters of exercise performance, including peak oxygen consumption (VO2, 28.8 [25.6-33.2] vs. 45.5 [41.7-49.9] ml/kg/min, p<0.0001) and peak work (192 [150-246] vs. 330 [209-402] Watts, p<0.0001), were lower in Fontan patients compared with controls. PAT ratio correlated with peak VO2 (r=0.28, p=0.02) and peak work (r=0.26, p=0.03). Conclusions: In asymptomatic Fontan patients, there is evidence of reduced basal peripheral arterial tone and vasodilator response, suggesting dysfunction of the endothelium-derived nitric oxide pathway. Vasodilator function appears to correlate modestly with exercise performance. Longitudinal study and assessment in a low-performing cohort are necessary to further evaluate the predictive value of endothelial pulse amplitude testing as an early marker of reduced exercise capacity in Fontan patients.

title: Mediterranean diet mediates the adverse effect of depressive symptomatology on short-term outcome in elderly survivors from an acute coronary event
abstract: Background: We evaluated the interaction between depressive symptoms and dietary habits on 30-day development of cardiovascular disease (CVD) (death or re-hospitalization) in elderly acute coronary syndrome (ACS) survivors.
